newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton, in Australia, says U.S. must look to East.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, in Australia, says U.S. must look to East.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton, on his first overseas trip since his re-election, met Australian leaders on Wednesday and reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the Asia-Pacific region.
On the first full day of a visit to Australia, Clinton laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, greeted crowds of well-wishers and met Prime Minister John Howard.
He was later to address a joint session of both houses of parliament and tell them the United States had to look East "no less than it looks to the West".

"I know that some people on both sides of the Pacific are concerned that America's continuing engagement with Europe will lead to disengagement from Asia," Clinton said in remarks prepared for delivery to the session. "They are wrong."

Clinton's message appeared primarily aimed at smoothing the ground for the main event of his nine-day Asia-Pacific visit -- a meeting with Chinese President Jiang Zemin in Manila on Sunday on the eve of a summit of regional leaders.
But it was guaranteed to go down well in Australia.
Canberra's ties with China have suffered since Howard's conservative coalition came to power in March.
Howard has said that Australia's ties with the the United States were neglected by his predecessor Paul Keating, who was too focused on relations with the country's neighbours in Asia.
That shift appears to have soured already patchy relations with China, which has accused Australia of being a pawn in an unstated U.S. policy of "containment".
Clinton said: "Mr Prime Minister, if I may borrow your eloquent words, the U.S. need not choose between our history and our geography. We need not choose between Europe and Asia."
"In a global economy with global security challenges, America must look to the East no less than it looks to the West."
Accompanied by wife Hillary, Clinton arrived in the Australian capital from Sydney aboard a U.S. Air Force Boeing 747 after a last-minute switch of aircraft.

White House officials said the Boeing 707 which was to have carried the president had communications equipment problems but denied earlier reports that there had been mechanical problems with the 30-year-old airplane.
"It's an aged plane with aged systems, but there was no issue of safety," a spokesman said.
The low-key visit is largely seen as a warm-up for Clinton's attendance at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in the Philippines next week.
Clinton extolled U.S.-Australia ties and make a reference to Australia's leading role in reviving a nuclear test ban treaty at the United Nations in September.

"Our two nations -- blessed by size, strength, prosperity, and the power of our example -- have a special responsibility to seize the opportunities of this time of change and to move steadily and strongly against the new threats change has produced," he said.

"Together, we can reduce even more the danger of weapons of mass destruction. We can take the fight to terrorists and drug traffickers. We can extend the reach of free and fair trade. We can advance democracy around the world," he said.
Apart from a speech to the Australian people from a site near the Sydney Opera House on Thursday, Clinton's schedule is largely free, allowing him time for at least one game of golf.
Australia's world number one Greg Norman and rising U.S. star Tiger Woods, both playing in a Sydney tournament, are obvious potential partners.

But Clinton expressed surprise at a report that he was travelling with a golf pro. "To my knowledge that is not so," he told reporters before going into his meeting with Howard. But he added: "I'm going to need all the help I can get tomorrow."
Keeping with the golf theme, Clinton and Howard discussed briefly the idea of establishing a golf competition pitting the best of Australia against the best of the United States.
The meeting itself was expected to focus on the more serious matters of trade and the role of the United States and Australia in Asia.
